subject: Archaeology
title: The Trowel: An Archaeologist's Best Friend
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Trowel: An Archaeologist's Best Friend.

hook.text: The most important tool in archaeology costs about $15 — a four-inch pointing trowel made by Marshalltown.

buildup.text: Archaeologists scrape soil in thin layers with the trowel's flat edge, feeling for changes in texture and hardness.

discovery.text: An experienced digger can feel the difference between a natural deposit and a filled-in pit just by trowel pressure.

twist.text: Worn-down trowels are badges of honor. Some archaeologists are buried with theirs.

climax.text: Despite drones, lasers, and satellites, the hand trowel has not been replaced. No machine can match a trained hand.

punchline.text: A $15 trowel outperforms satellites when precision matters most.

quiz.question: Why hasn't the hand trowel been replaced by modern technology?
options: Budget constraints prevent most digs from using advanced equipment
No machine can match a trained hand at detecting subtle soil changes
Regulations require all excavation to be done with traditional tools

details.summary: The pointing trowel is the archaeologist's primary excavation tool — a small, flat-bladed implement used to carefully scrape soil in thin layers. Skilled troweling reveals color and texture changes invisible to less delicate tools, exposing features, floors, and interfaces between deposits.
details.whyItMatters: The trowel represents archaeology's commitment to precision over speed. Choosing a hand tool over heavy machinery for fine work reflects the discipline's core principle that context is more valuable than the objects themselves.
takeaways: The pointing trowel is the primary hand excavation tool
Skilled troweling reveals subtle soil changes invisible to machines
It symbolizes archaeology's commitment to precision and context

faq.question: Why do archaeologists prefer trowels over larger tools?
faq.answer: Trowels allow the excavator to feel changes in soil density and texture while scraping. This tactile feedback helps identify features like post holes, floors, and pit edges that would be destroyed by larger tools. The flat blade creates clean surfaces for photography and recording.

faq.question: What brand of trowel do most archaeologists prefer?
faq.answer: The Marshalltown trowel is the industry standard in much of the English-speaking world. Its 4-inch or 5-inch pointing trowel has a tempered steel blade that holds an edge well. Archaeologists often keep the same trowel for their entire career, resharpening it until the blade is worn thin.
